In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the Cordilleras Darwin and Darwin icefield (CDI) in southern Patagonia, Chile (54º S), during the Holocene.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CDI glaciers were land-based during the first part (before 12,300 years BP) of the Holocene.
the Holocene fluctuations in the CDI glaciers were not in phase with the fluctuations in the SPI glaciers, but rather with those in the Northern Patagonian Icefields.
the CDI glaciers were land-based during the early Holocene and advanced during the Neoglacial period.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Cordillera Darwins glaciers have not been land based for at least the last 14,300 cal years.
the Cordillera is a very dynamic place with respect to its glaciers, and this is a place that is going to be very sensitive to changes in global climate.
the Holocene fluctuations in Cordillera Darwin were not only less pronounced than those of the Neoglacial but also out-of-phase with the Southern Patagonia Icefield (SPI).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Holocene glacier evolution in the CDI was different from the SPI, with the latter experiencing more glacier fluctuations and larger ice volumes.

the current land-terminating situation of most CDI glaciers, as well as the associated glaciolacustrine sedimentary deposits, are not unique to the modern period but have been present for most of the Holocene.
the modern transition of most CDI glaciers to land-based conditions may be a unique feature of modern climate conditions.
